subtopics.description: Definition of linearity and the superposition principle. Comparison with common non-linear phenomena (quadratic growth, exponential decay). Motivation for why linear models are tractable and widely used in engineering and data science.

subtopics.subtopic_name: Real-life examples and applications of linear algebra
subtopics.description: Overview of application domains where linear algebra plays a central role: search engine ranking (Google PageRank), navigation and shortest-path mapping, machine learning, image processing, and economics. Emphasis on how linear structures simplify complex problems.

topics.learning_intent: Students will be able to distinguish linear from non-linear relationships, understand the role of linearity in modeling real-world problems, and recognize how linear algebra concepts like PageRank and Google Maps routing apply to practical engineering and data science scenarios.

subtopics.description: Introduction to n-dimensional vectors, vector addition, scalar multiplication, and linear combination of vectors. Geometric interpretation in 2D and 3D. Writing a system of equations as a vector equation and as a matrix-vector product.

Graphical representation of linear equations in two and three variables. Intersecting lines, planes, and the geometric meaning of unique, infinite, and no solutions. Row picture versus column picture of a system.

Gaussian elimination and Gauss-Jordan elimination as systematic solving procedures. Row operations, leading variables, free variables, and identification of the rank of a matrix. Connection between rank and the number of solutions.
Row echelon form and reduced row echelon form (RREF). Pivots, back-substitution, and converting any matrix to RREF. Elementary matrices and their role in representing row operations.

Distinction between homogeneous (Ax = 0) and non-homogeneous (Ax = b) systems. Null space (kernel) of a matrix. Solution sets: trivial, infinite, and empty. Conditions for consistency in non-homogeneous systems.

subtopics.subtopic_name: Applications of systems of linear equations
subtopics.description: Applications in machine learning (linear regression setup), cryptography (encoding/decoding messages), and color models in digital imaging (RGB and CMY representations). Worked examples for each domain.

topics.learning_intent: Students will be able to represent and solve systems of linear equations using vector and matrix notation, perform row reduction to determine rank and solution type, and apply these techniques to model and solve problems in machine learning, cryptography, and color representation.

subtopics.description: Axiomatic definition of a vector space over R (and extension to C). Subspaces: definition, tests for subspace, examples (null space, column space, span of a set). Practical examples from R^n and function spaces.

Linear combination and linear span of a set of vectors. Linear independence and dependence: definition, geometric interpretation, and connection to homogeneous systems. Spanning sets and minimal spanning sets. Basis of a vector space, coordinates of a vector relative to a basis, and the standard basis.

Dimension as the cardinality of any basis. Dimension theorem: dimension of a vector space equals the number of vectors in any basis. Rank-nullity theorem for linear transformations: dim(domain) = dim(kernel) + dim(image). Applications to solving linear systems.

Definition of linear transformation between vector spaces. Kernel (null space) and image (range) of a linear transformation. One-to-one and onto transformations. Classification of linear transformations as singular or non-singular (invertible).

subtopics.subtopic_name: Matrix representations, similarity, and change of basis
subtopics.description: Matrix representation of a linear transformation given a basis. Similar matrices represent the same linear transformation in different bases. Change of basis matrix. Diagonal representation of a linear operator when possible. Introduction to matrix similarity.

subtopics.subtopic_name: Inner product spaces, orthogonality, and Gram-Schmidt
subtopics.description: Inner product on R^n and general inner product spaces. Norm induced by an inner product. Orthogonality and orthogonal complements. Orthogonal sets and orthonormal bases. Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process with worked numerical examples.
prerequisites_within_course: Matrix representations, similarity, and change of basis

topics.learning_intent: Students will be able to define and work with vector spaces, identify subspaces, determine linear independence and basis, and apply linear transformations to map between vector spaces. They will understand the rank-nullity theorem and be able to compute orthonormal bases using the Gram-Schmidt process for applications in data smoothing and image scaling.

subtopics.description: Characteristic equation det(A - λI) = 0. Trace and determinant in terms of eigenvalues. Multiplicity of eigenvalues (algebraic and geometric). Cayley-Hamilton theorem: every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, enabling evaluation of matrix polynomials.

Definition of eigenvector and eigenvalue. Geometric interpretation: eigenvectors as directions that remain unchanged (scaled) by the transformation. Visualization of stretching and rotation in R^2. Eigenspaces.

Diagonalizable matrices: definition and sufficient condition (n linearly independent eigenvectors). Procedure for diagonalization A = PDP^{-1}. Computing A^k for large k using diagonalization. Functions of matrices such as e^{At} using diagonalization.

Properties of symmetric matrices: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors. Real spectral theorem for symmetric matrices: A = QDQ^T where Q is orthogonal. Connection between symmetry and diagonalization with orthogonal matrices.

subtopics.subtopic_name: Quadratic forms and least squares method
subtopics.description: Quadratic forms x^T Ax. Change of variables to eliminate cross terms (principal axis theorem). Classification: positive definite, negative definite, indefinite. Least squares approximation: normal equations, projection onto subspace, and geometric interpretation. Applications in curve fitting and data fitting.

topics.learning_intent: Students will be able to compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalize matrices, and apply these concepts to analyze symmetric matrices, classify quadratic forms, and solve least squares problems for applications in facial recognition, feature extraction, and search engines.

subtopics.description: Review of eigendecomposition for symmetric matrices. Limitations of eigenvalue decomposition for non-square and non-symmetric matrices. Need for a general matrix factorization. Connection between eigenvalues and singular values.
prerequisites_within_course: Quadratic forms and least squares method

subtopics.description: SVD theorem: A = UΣV^T where U and V are orthogonal matrices and Σ is a diagonal matrix of singular values. Relationship between singular values and eigenvalues of A^TA. Construction of U and V from left and right singular vectors. Full and reduced SVD forms.

Low-rank approximation using truncated SVD. Eckart-Young theorem: best rank-k approximation in Frobenius norm is given by truncating SVD. Interpretation of singular values as energy in data. Application to image compression.

Power iteration for computing the dominant eigenvalue and eigenvector. Extension to singular values via A^TA. Convergence behavior, dominant singular value separation, and practical implementation. Limitations for ill-conditioned matrices.

subtopics.subtopic_name: Applications: PCA, document ranking, and clustering
subtopics.description: Principal component analysis as an application of SVD: centering data, computing covariance matrix, extracting principal components. Data centering and its role in PCA. Document-term matrices and Latent Semantic Analysis for document ranking. Connection between SVD and k-means clustering.

topics.learning_intent: Students will be able to perform and interpret singular value decomposition, use rank-k approximations to compress data, apply the power method for approximating dominant singular values, and employ PCA and related techniques for dimensionality reduction, document ranking, and clustering in data science contexts.

subtopics.description: Formulation and solving of traffic flow problems using systems of linear equations (conservation of vehicles at junctions). Kirchhoff's laws and circuit analysis using linear systems. Worked examples for both applications.

subtopics.subtopic_name: Chemical equation balancing and data compression
subtopics.description: Balancing chemical equations as a linear algebra problem (setting up and solving systems over integers). Data compression using SVD-based rank-k approximation on image and signal data, with comparison of compression ratio and reconstruction error.
prerequisites_within_course: Chemical equation balancing and data compression

subtopics.subtopic_name: Word embeddings, bias in data, and Markov matrices
subtopics.description: Representation of words as vectors using embedding techniques and their properties (similarity, analogy). Detection and impact of bias in high-dimensional data through linear algebra. Markov matrices: transition matrices, steady-state vectors, and application to PageRank algorithm.
prerequisites_within_course: Word embeddings, bias in data, and Markov matrices

subtopics.description: Two-player zero-sum games modeled as payoff matrices. Determining optimal strategies using linear programming concepts. Introduction to information retrieval as vector space search: term-document matrices, cosine similarity, and relevance ranking.

subtopics.subtopic_name: Specialized applications: chessboard moves and genetics modeling
subtopics.description: Knight's tour problem and chessboard move modeling using state-space representation and linear recurrences. Genetics modeling: inheritance patterns, population dynamics matrices, Leslie matrices in demography, and Markov chain models for gene sequencing.
prerequisites_within_course: Specialized applications: chessboard moves and genetics modeling

topics.learning_intent: Students will be able to apply linear algebra techniques across a range of engineering and data science domains, including traffic flow modeling, circuit analysis, chemical balancing, data compression, word embeddings, information retrieval, and genetic modeling. They will understand the role of Markov matrices in PageRank and can analyze game strategies using payoff matrices.

syllabus.coverage_summary: This undergraduate Linear Algebra course covers six interconnected units spanning 45 contact hours across one semester. The course begins by establishing the conceptual importance of linearity and its applications (Unit I), then builds a strong foundation in solving systems of linear equations using vector-matrix methods, row elimination, and rank analysis (Unit II). Unit III develops the abstract theory of vector spaces including subspaces, linear independence, basis, dimension, linear transformations, and the rank-nullity theorem, culminating in inner product spaces and the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process. Unit IV focuses on eigenvalues and eigenvectors with emphasis on the characteristic polynomial, Cayley-Hamilton theorem, diagonalization, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms, and the least squares method. Unit V introduces singular value decomposition (SVD) as a generalization of eigenvalue decomposition, covering spectral decomposition, rank-k approximation, the power method, and applications in PCA, document ranking, and clustering. Unit VI consolidates the course through extensive real-world applications including traffic systems, circuit analysis, chemical balancing, data compression, word embeddings, Markov matrices and PageRank, game strategies, information retrieval, and genetics modeling. The course maintains a balance between conceptual understanding, computational proficiency, and application across disciplines consistent with undergraduate-level expectations.
